game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is interesting, the UI is fantastic, but...

The writing doesn't work. Not to me, at least.

So the idea is, you're an anonymous member of the public working with a new program that's half google, half snooping software. You're assigned a case - the first one is about a bomb placed in a plaza, and thanks to surveillance cameras you're assigned to look up everything about a suspect. So far so good, right? There's the relevant question of whether it's right to spy on someone in the name of public safety, there's a mystery to solve...

But it falls apart. Your supervisor is all "she has a police record, let's snoop on her" and okay, good enough reason to investigate...her faux-facebook page, her faux-portfolio, news websites, etcetera. Except that none of these websites feel like they were ever used by real people, her facebook timeline feels bizarre, like she's a fascimile of a human being, and when you get to eavesdrop on her text messages with her boyfriend, again it feels false?

Everything is off, and not in a good way. And your supervisor is so ready to pin the entire case on her because she's joined an activist group that organizes protests against the surveillance state.

It's too on the nose, with writing that doesn't sell to me that I'm snooping on real people, with a wonky "this is taking place in real time" - but it's not, really, you only get to eavesdrop on people's text conversations when you unlock them, not when they happen - and it all just feels clumsy.

In a game that's only got its writing going for it, having a fantastically slick UI isn't going to keep me playing it. Which is a bummer! The questions this game is asking are relevant, and it's so slick and pretty to look at I want to dig into it! ... But sadly it's just not compelling.

Bummer.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
With "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" Osmotic Studios and publisher Daedalic Entertainment deliver a narrative surveillance thriller that quietly turns its own core theme into self parody. The player is asked to watch over the privacy of others, while in the background a telemetry chain made of Steam, Unity and Mailchimp wakes up, of which not a single word can be found on the product page.

[h1]What does the product do?[/h1]On first launch the game already talks to Steam, fetches the SDR config for AppID 491950. In parallel Unity reaches out to Google Cloud, generates a persistent userid and ships a full hardware profile. Only after all of this does the player see a brief in game pointer to an external privacy notice.

[h1]Who operates the product?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH (formerly Fellow Traveller)
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH (current publisher)

[h1]Which service providers are involved?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH
Valve Corporation
Unity Technologies
Google, LLC (infrastructure for Unity)
Intuit Mailchimp (owned by Intuit Inc.)
[noparse]Amazon.com, Inc.[/noparse]

[h1]What data is collected?[/h1]
Unique identifiers have been redacted for the review.
[b]Unity Analytics (no visible notice)[/b]
Unity 6000.3.8f1 fires POST requests to the Unity Analytics config and event endpoints. The endpoints resolve to Google Cloud in the United States.
[list][*] Persistent userid and deviceid, sessionid, session_count
[*] appid and build_guid
[*] Full hardware profile: CPU, RAM, VRAM, GPU vendor, driver, D3D12 feature level
[*] OS version, language, mainboard model, machine hostname
[*] Events appStart, appStop, SubsystemInfo, shaderRuntimeInfo
[/list]No OptIn is shown, tracking cannot be turned off inside the game.

[b]Steam Datagram Relay[/b]
The client fetches the Steam SDR configuration for the game and then opens 34 UDP connections to Frankfurt, Stockholm, London, Paris, Vienna, Warsaw, Amsterdam, New York, Chicago, Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles, Seattle, Sao Paulo, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Hong Kong, Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Mumbai, Sydney, Johannesburg and Dubai. For a pure single player thriller this fanout provides no benefit.

[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
The in game newsletter sends first name, email and the tag "Orwell" straight to the Mailchimp REST API. The client uses a fixed HTTP Basic Auth credential baked into the build, "user:[redacted]-us14", which is a full Mailchimp API key visible in any network capture. The server response leaks list metadata, sender, statistics and a contact address (Papenstrasse 27, 22089 Hamburg) that differs from the one in the privacy notice. Headers reveal hosting in AWS us east 2.

[h1]GDPR violations in detail[/h1]
[b]Unity Analytics without consent[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)a Transparency: Transmission starts before the user is informed
[*] Art. 6 Lawfulness: No consent, no documented legitimate interest
[*] Art. 7 Consent: No OptIn dialog, the pointer arrives too late
[*] Art. 13 Information obligation: Unity Analytics and Google Cloud are not named
[*] Art. 25 Privacy by Design: Tracking is default, no in game switch
[*] Art. 44ff Third country transfer: US Google Cloud, no SCC notice in game
[/list]
[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)f Integrity: The API key sits in plain text in the game binary
[*] Art. 13: Hosting in the US is not disclosed in game
[*] Art. 25: No server side email validation
[*] Art. 44ff: Third country transfer to the US, no visible safeguard
[/list]
[b]Steam SDR[/b]
Art. 5(1)c Data minimization: 34 worldwide relays for a solo title are excessive.

[h1]Privacy policy and Opt-in/Opt-out[/h1]
The Steam product page does not show or link any privacy policy or EULA. Inside the game a short pointer appears during profile creation, but only after Steam SDR and Unity have already shipped data abroad. The Steam age rating in Germany is "12 and up" while the Osmotic privacy notice itself requires a minimum age of 18. No age verification takes place.

A second oversight: the in game privacy notice is supposed to exist in English and German. In reality the "German" file is a word for word copy of the English text, only the headline reads "Datenschutzerklärung". A German speaking user has no proper localized notice available in game, which under Art. 12 GDPR is a serious flaw.

The notice itself does not name Unity Analytics, does not mention the Google Cloud infrastructure, does not list the Mailchimp pipeline and says nothing about a hardcoded API key inside the client.

[h1]Can this behavior be blocked?[/h1]
Yes, largely. The Unity Analytics endpoints, the Mailchimp REST API and the Steam SDR config request can all be blocked at the network layer without breaking gameplay. "Orwell" is a pure single player title, neither Unity Analytics nor SDR are required for it to run.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" stages a surveillance state and trains the player to quietly oversee the data of strangers, while at the same time keeping a close eye inside its own engine room.

The Steam product page skips any data protection or EULA information, the in game pointer arrives too late and in a language version that is German only by name. Unity Analytics runs without a visible OptIn through Google Cloud in the United States, the newsletter pipeline goes through Mailchimp with an API key baked into the client, and Steam SDR opens 34 UDP connections worldwide for a solo title.

The thematic punch line lands twice here, once in the script and once in the network log.

[h1]Additional Info[/h1]
Additional details, including a full connection overview for blocking access, involved IPv4 addresses, company information and the German version of the review, are available as usual at [url=https://gameindustry.eu]GameIndustry[/url]. If you're interested, join the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/penguindome]Penguin Domination[/url] group to stay informed about new reviews on Steam.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm stopping because of the mechanic: Conflicted Datachunks.

You're presented two conflicting stories and have to choose which is true.  It's fun when you can figure out why the stories conflict. Most of the time, though, there's not enough evidence.  And once you make a choice - there's no going back.

This is opposite of how we should handle conflictings ideas. It's important to avoid jumping to conclusions - something your counterpart Symes does consistently. It's important to be open to possibilities and revise your position if new valid evidence comes in.

We're all subject to confirmation bias - games can teach us how to recognize and manage it.  "Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments" is a better model for dealing with difficult, uncertain decisions.

I'm happy Osmotic Studios is tackling such weighty topics in their games, but it also means the skills the player practices need to build solid foundations for dealing with those issues.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Drag-and-Drop Simulator. Interactive story at best - not much for a point-and-click adventure.

Owell isn't the first "surveillance sim", and certainly isn't the best. It does plenty of things right, but far more wrong. Because of that, while I enjoyed the game and didn't feel the gameplay bad - I can't recommend it. 

The game holds your hand literally the entire way. It highlights information. It tells you when you've looked over a document and missed something. It repeats the obvious to you via your "advisor", Symes. It doesn't encourage reading whatsoever despite it only having pros as an interactive story.

One of the most irritating things of the game was Symes. Symes is your advisor through the game, commenting on evidence you find. The problem is that he comments on Ever. Little. Piece. of evidence. If you add someone's favorite color - Symes chimes in. If you add a new profile picture for a person - he has something SO IMPORTANT to say that it stops gameplay until you click continue. Again and again and again. 

Other elements of the game leave you wishing you were more in control of the program. For example, I wanted the ability to create profiles on people but you aren't given that permission. Symes gives you permission when you reach a certain point in the story, and that's that. I wanted to add a profile picture for someone I had a profile on..... NOPE couldn't do it until the game gives you permission to.

The game really gives you the illusion of control while the entire time you are limited to dragging and dropping story elements. The conflicts in data are VERY minor and ultimately the story wraps up in a similar way either way. It's the feeling of diverse while being completely linear. In the instances where there WERE conflicts in data, you really have to take a shot in the dark sometimes. 

So what did I expect? I wanted to be in charge of the note taking! I wanted to be able to create profiles on my own. I didn't want information to get highlighted for me UNLESS there was a problem. I wanted to be able to figure things out the entire time without some doofus interrupting gameplay the entire time with his commentary (Symes). 

Still, there are certainly pros to give this game. The story is interesting, the graphics are BEAUTIFUL for the genre, and the point-and-click adventure feel is definitely there, even if the game leads you where you need to go. Browse websites and news articles as though you were in your very own web browser! Now that I say that in writing, it doesn't seem all that impressive, but it's still enjoyable. The "accessing computer" elements and phone conversation elements I enjoy so much more than the web browsing.

All in all, it's an interesting point-and-click interactive story with multiple outcomes. It's not a difficult one, and there are no puzzles to solve, so just sit back and enjoy it. I still can't recommend it to anyone who is a fan of hacksims, surveillance sims, or information gathering sims though.... this is an interactive story - nothing more. It's no more "investigatory" than any of the TellTale games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While the game is beautiful and handcrafted I cannot recommend it due to a bug in the game that risks a potential hazard to your computer hardware.

1st: the game keeps generating new internet permission requests in my firewall which io keep denying.
A single player game has no buisness attempting to connect to the internet.

2nd there are cases that when upon denying these requests the game will cause some weird IRQ conflict error that crashes your graphics card. (I will also note that i never had a game cause an IRQ conflict upon denying an internet request via my firewall before, this game is the first game i encountered to cause such a thing)

I have a threadripper 1950x and an RTX 2080TI, when I tried to launch the game after it crashed to desktop, it crashed to desktop again. and all my other games expirenced the same issue even though the graphics card was still registered in my system. but during these crashes my fan speeds would reset to default.

upon rebooting i could play everything normally again and then when I launched orwell again and denied the new internet request, crash to desktop, and persistent crashes in every other game till i rebooted.

I dont know why a single player game needs an internet connection, or what its doing that is causing an IRQ conflict so bad that it crashes my graphics card.

But i cannot recommend this game in good faith because of the severity of the crash it causes. it may not happen every time, nor will it likey happen on every system configuration but I refuse to recommend a game that causes an IRQ conflict on ANY system for ANY reason.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While the story is interesting and I can see replayability in knowing you've made the wrong move, then creating a new profile and trying to avoid that scenario... I haven't done that. I probably won't either, because I have to agree with other players: the game guides you too much.

You're basically told where to click and when, which completely defeats the point of having all of these fun tools at your disposal--they might as well have dumped all data pieces in a list and had you click on them one by one, all after the other.

The auto-highlighting spoils the point of reading anything. The game warns you that potential choices conflict instead of letting the player decide on how thoroughly they want to investigate before submitting information. Some pieces of info feel completely useless, but your supervisor somehow decides they have more value than they should and the supervisor's decision often feels like a complete whim. And vice-versa: bits of info you feel should be important are locked away or not even meant to be accessible because the game decided "Nope, I won't even let you go into that dead-end for fun".

I guess this was worth what I paid for it... $2! and no more. This had a lot of promise but it doesn't have enough depth or freedom of choice for my tastes.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" seems content to repeat what books and movies have said more eloquently.  It also falls below the dollar per hour metric (it can be completed within 5 hours).

The gameplay is simple and involves clicking through fake internet websites, blogs, and chat logs to collect bits of information (a process that can easily become tedious).

So the appeal is obviously the story, but for $9.99, you're better off buying a copy of George Orwell's 1984, or Aldous Huxley's Brave New World instead. This game is nothing more than a shallow summary of the themes explored in depth by those literary works.

Unity engine build: 2018.3.0f2. There were some graphical issues with the native Linux version. Solved by using Proton.

review_text_raw:
[h1][i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye One You’s[/i] centrism recklessly justifies surveillance[/h1]

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] (Osmotic Studios, 2016) should not have to prove that mass surveillance is a public danger. Lifting the name of one of the 20th century’s most enduring authors, [i]Orwell[/i] reverses the traditional dystopian power dynamic by casting the player as an investigator utilizing government software to snoop on anyone deemed potentially dangerous to the state. The setup is almost too clean to be proper satire, too on the nose to spark the outrage necessary to criticize what is fast becoming a common aspect of life.

Across the globe, [url=https://www.amnesty.org.uk/north-korea-surveillance-state-prison-camp-internet-phone-technology]authoritarian[/url] and [url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/national-security/cia-crypto-encryption-machines-espionage/]democratic governments[/url] alike have begun [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/9kx4z8/revealed-this-is-palantirs-top-secret-user-manual-for-cops?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]adopting surveillance technology[/url] under the [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/k7exem/banjo-ai-company-utah-surveillance-panopticon?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]premise of reducing crime[/url]. Few of these programs have detailed exactly what data is being collected and how it is being used, but journalists have exposed many of the ways surveillance programs are only [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/05/technology/clearview-investors.html?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]further stratifying power along class[/url] and [url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/612876/this-is-how-ai-bias-really-happensand-why-its-so-hard-to-fix/]racial lines[/url]. The dystopia is already here. The role of fiction is no longer to provide warnings and speculation, it’s to interrogate our current reality.

[i]Orwell[/i] released less than five years ago, but it is shocking how tame its surveillance state looks compared to how corporations and governments are currently operating (and in all likelihood, how they were spying in years prior). For starters, its system is structured to rely on human intuition rather than artificial intelligence. Data points are only considered after they’ve been entered by the investigator, after which supervisors are required to act upon them even to the point of self-incrimination.

Orwell, the program, is portrayed as an equalizing arbiter of justice. Only late in the game is the idea floated that the investigators are being watched too. But by that time the system has already been a resounding success. Lives have been saved and poorly coordinating terrorists are behind bars. If [i]Orwell[/i] intended to question the merit of a nationwide police state, it accidentally proved the other side’s point. In this reality, the only reason to oppose surveillance is that it feels icky to have your phones tapped and your computers bugged.

But this isn’t how surveillance functions, or how these systems are run. Almost universally, modern surveillance technology is autonomous, relying on millions of data points to infer what the system believes a crime to be. This has enormous ramifications when the criminal justice [url=http://inthesetimes.com/working/entry/17505/police_and_poor_people]system disproportionally targets people of color and the poor[/url]. Facial recognition has already been proven to possess the same biases as the system utilizing it, which is to say nothing of the exceptions granted to the wealthy and other members of power.

In [i]Orwell*, the terrorists are strictly ideological. They are educated, wealthy, white, heterosexual philosophers waging a war of ideas that almost by accident turns violent. These people exist, sure, but they are not the ones targeted by surveillance systems. That *Orwell[/i] utterly ignores any possibility of racial and ethnic biases or the role history plays in policing, renders the whole game hollow and borderline optimistic. None of the characters the player investigates are innocent. Orwell is infallible, even if its implementation is unnerving.

The final bizarre and revealing element [i]Orwell[/i] is how little it allows the player to deviate from what the system believes to be relevant. Play involves parsing documents and dragging relevant information over to profiles, but the only pieces of data which can be included are ones the game has highlighted in advance.

This begs the question as to why the player is there. Is it to catch the extremely rare instance of irrelevant data being entered into the system (ie. a person’s favorite color)? If so, why does the supervisor ultimately decide what is and isn’t relevant? Are they meant to be an impartial judge of the people being investigated? Why, then, does the system decide what information can be considered in a case?

[i]Orwell[/i] tries to introduce safeguards into the surveillance operation but in doing so further highlights how futile these measures are in protecting from false imprisonment and machine bias. If we are beginning the conversation at “how do we ethically implement a mass surveillance system” we have already lost. It is not a question of how it can be done, it is a question of how we could allow it to happen. These systems exist. They are being used. Hell, even [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/19/opinion/facebook-cambridge-analytica.html]Facebook operates in ways indistinguishable from police surveillance[/url] and might be more successful for it.

Games like [i]Orwell[/i] recklessly attempt to work backward from the lies used to justify surveillance, rather than recognizing that we have to fight the concept itself. It is a game decades too late to matter and does more to legitimize its target than it does to take them down.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Here's what happens: You get told to look up this woman who may have commited a crime. You don't actually look up anything, you just click on the page it gives you. It highlights what in that page you are supposed to save. It tells you when you have collected all of the information from that page and moves on to the next one. The entire game is just looking at these pages, or conversations, and dragging highlighted text or photos to a folder. That's it.
This game doesn't require thinking, not really. I thought the fact that you could choose what text you send over meant you could omit anything you wanted, but then it won't move on to the next series of pages. You have to send it something, and it pretty much all leads to the same outcomes.
It could have been a lot better. If it wasn't so linear, if you were left to search and find things on your own, if you could pick out which people to build a dossier on, anything like that would have made this awesome.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't feel like I can truly call this a detective game, or even a puzzle game. The choices available are limited (2-3 outcomes), and [spoiler] almost none of the choices that are made throughout the game affect the ending, or really the flow of the story in general[/spoiler]. Choices do not matter. [spoiler] Speaking of the ending, I felt that they were quite sudden, especially "Thoughts are free", and didn't follow entirely plausibly from the actions you took to get there. How exactly does the investigator incriminating oneself IMMEDIATELY result in the termination of Orwell? How does an incredibly sophisticated surveillance program like Orwell, even still in test phase, get torn down in a day? Never mind that there were probably backup investigators lined up, or that The Party likely would not have wanted to let go of the project so easily. If the main message of the story is that "surveillance cannot be impartial and bias will always be present", then it seems careless to throw away the secondary message - "surveillance is pervasive and nigh impossible to detect and curtail once it reaches a tipping point" - in the final moment. And yet curtail in an instant, they did. [/spoiler]

Credit where it is due, the character dialogue and writings felt very genuine, and portrayed each person convincingly.

Other reviewers have already said all of this, better. Like [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/MangoMaraudr/recommended/491950/]this one[/url].

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell has a compelling story set in a dystopian maybe-not-so-future where the government has begun a program to monitor any and everything in real time.

The story was very good, however, to experience all of the options you have to replay the full game. There are several 7+ minute conversations paced out painfully slowly. I get that the pacing is set to make it feel like you're monitoring this real time (and that's important in a few cases!) but the majority of the time, pretty much any time there isn't tense music going on, the game needs an option to skip through the snoozefest that is the communications system. I legitimately got up, made myself a meal, and came back to find one segment still running. What was an engaging and interesting storyline the first time around became a complete drag by the end.

If you're not a lore-focused gamer, you'll hate this game. If you're a fast reader, you'll hate this game. If you're a slow reader who likes good stories, this is the game for you.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell fails on a lot of levels. A lot of very fundamental writing levels. First and foremost it gives you a set of tools that allow you to see what people do on the internet and tasks you with finding the perpetrator of a bombing. You're given one prime suspect and as you progress your web of people of interest grows and grows. The principle gameplay mechanic involves choosing which specific pieces of information you choose to report to your orwellian system. Which will change how the game plays out. The first failure comes that it is often very obvious what information is going to affect what, as it is all highlighted in blue, or yellow if it conflicts with another piece of information. This is another problem. The conflict system makes very little sense most of the time. One of the first examples of the system in use involves a personal blog ran by a Person of Interest and an editorial they wrote for a newspaper. They both detail the same concept but with completely differeing opinions on the matter, and these pieces of information are considered a conflict and therefore cannot both be reported. While this specific instance makes very little gameplay difference either way it still makes no sense. Being able to report both pieces of information would have shown (at least to me) his willingness to play whatever side of an issue would get him paid, and could've sowed him as a much stronger suspect later on. Instead you have instances where you handler is confused by information you weren't able to provide them due to it being a conflict, when both pieces of information were true. This creates a very frustrating experience in trying to influence the story and with trying to keep information that is relevant to the story seperate from information that isnt. Another fundamental failing of the story telling is its ending, which if I'm perfectly honest; is godawful. To my knowledge, your choices throughout the game have no impact on the ending. There's just three buttons at the end. Push one for your ending. None of them making  a bit of sense. Right before your ending the perpetrator of the bombings reveals themselves, showing that the previous three chapters had all just been misdirection to make sure no player could possibly guess the real one and they basically say to you the player "And this is why your system doesn't work! You couldn't even figure out I was the perpetrator" When it was the game mechanics and information that was provided to you by the game that made it impossible to determine the perpetrator. They then ask you to take down the system, since you can now see it doesnt work. your other two options are to get a politician associated with your orwell system arrested, or to claim the group the perpetrator belongs to are all terrorists using out of context IMs. If you're thinking that this seems to be lacking a very obvious fourth option then I agree. My first instinct was simply to use the perpetrator admitting to instigating the bombings to get her arrested. As that would make sense, she admitted it to our face and yet there's no option present. Just the three arbitrary ones presented. In the end it was three chapters of intriguing build up for one chapter of letdowns and unguessable twists that completely kill the narrative, suspension of disbelief, and immersion. 4/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is one of the few I don’t really feel I can fall down on either side. Ultimately, I felt I should mark it as unrecommended because I couldn’t bring myself to give it a thumbs up, and steam doesn’t have a ‘meh, its ok I guess’ option.

The story is, literally as it is titled, an Orwellian style, drama, I guess. Unfortunately the railroading detracts from the telling. 

The game play is actually pretty good and quite well done. As an investigator you’re expected to dig up as much information as you can regarding suspects in a terrorist attack, and then use their connections and the information gleaned to unpick what occurred and who is responsible, with the ultimate aim of preventing another attack. It is actually the limitations that are forced upon you to ensure you don’t get lost, combined with the multitude of ‘coincidences’ and other sloppy writing that only drives the story in a railroaded direction that bring the whole thing down.

Pros:
The game is easy to play, for the most part allows you to take your time reading the information and make your decision. The way the information is presented is also easy to digest and use. 
The characters are each unique and seem quite well thought out with their own motivations and histories. They also have an interesting dynamic that shows the growth, depth, and fading of their friendship as natural friendships have done.


Cons: 
The game opens with a single character to investigate, while that makes sense from a tutorial point, it doesn’t from a story point. This then focus and railroading leading to a contrived conclusion full of plot holes and excuses kinda ruins the game.
The system showcases a really interesting idea for ways to gather and profile information, monitor suspects, and use what you learn to further an investigation. Then it doesn’t let you do it, restricting what you can see to only a tiny window. It makes for a surveillance system that can’t watch anything.
Tying in to the above, we have so much information on the characters, but can’t utilise any of the information we would undoubtedly be able to access as law enforcement. Once again it felt like an artificial restriction, which was most frustrating.

Suggested improvements:
A skip dialogue button. Most of the few hours I’ve racked up were waiting for conversations to end.
Allow the system to access some of the surveyed individual’s data and build the puzzle environment that way.
Allow us to use the system in the ways we feel fit, not just the way that gives the narrative held.
For the love of god, let us investigate more people, more red herrings. Let us be the ones to cross off people from the lists, let us be the ones that decide what’s worth pursuing. 

Overall Recommendation:
This game has so much potential as a story driven and person centred hook. Especially for people who enjoy info hunts or detective style games. I can see it being really expandable with so many story options.
I think if you like that kind of game, this will scratch an itch for you.
But I can’t recommend it in its current state. As it is it comes off negatively and that just spoils all of the good things about it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a joke of a government surveillance program and you are the operator. Luckily, I got the game for free.

I have no idea why it got so many positive reviews. I understand the game is a fresh take into 'investigative work' but it's not L.A. Noire. The game is so simplified, it gives an impression that solving crime is that easy. 

Your job is to solve crime by sitting at your desk, waiting for info or evidence from sources such as the 'leading newspaper', websites, emails, phone calls and insiders. I can understand tapping calls and emails but getting direct info from the government newspaper is questionable. Most of the info doesn't need to be verified. 

The game has 2 main problems:
Firstly, all the info/evidences from the sources are highlighted for you!! No need to read much. You just need to click, drag and drop into different profiles. That's your job, I swear! Geez!!

Secondly, when new info/evidence pops up, you can't override the old ones in the Orwell database. What?? Sigh.

At the time of writing, I have yet to finish the game. It's really painful to continue but I will try. In my opinion, totally not worth the time if you really want true blue investigative work. Buy L.A. Noire instead.

Terrible game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
As a game, it's way too scripted and practically visual novel -like, allowing practically no freedom of action for the player in what is presented as an interactive plot system.

Orwell does present a good criticism of government security and crime-fighting total surveillance programs that have been popping up around the world for at least the last decade. The story highlights many of the fundamental issues with such programs. It's just a pity that the story experience is ruined by the restrictive gameplay system, that forces you to do things in a silly way and backtrack to earlier data sources to use data blocks only later unlocked..

A key plot device element that got totally overlooked in the game design is that an attentive player could turn the use of the Orwell system on its head quite early on significantly affecting the story outcome to fit the canon narrative, but this is simply not possible in the game.

It is fun with nice story. Completed in 4 hrs, with an additional 2 hrs for a few more achievements. The story line is linear thus not much replay value. Whether you choose to free or jail or kill a characters does not affect subsequent stories.

Surveillance is only a means for the ends. In 1984, war is a tool to maintain power. Who cares about a little bomb and civilian casualties? In such a world, you don't catch terrorists but political enemies (then called them terrorists in news report). 

Half way through the game when I was going after real bomb terrorists, I thought I am in the prologue and wondering why the tutorial took so long. Also, because of 1984 I expected the "twist". I think I would vote for "yes" if it does not relates itself with 1984.

ps. The government in the game is really decent and ideal. It arrest and prosecute according to evidence.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In Orwell you sit in front of a virtual computer screen and attempt to track down the perpetrators of a recent bombing in an authoritarian surveillance state (hence the name of the game).

Set in the fictitious country of The Nation, you play The Investigator, someone employed from outside The Nation to work on its secret interior security project called Orwell. You receive verbal communiques one-way from your supervisor, who directs you on what to do. In return you send back snippets of information you find online.

In the aftermath of a bombing in Freedom Plaza (ironic name, geddit?), you must track down the perpetrators. You start from a single person arrested at the scene, and trace out her social and familial connections to bring more and more people under scrutiny. 

The Orwell computer system allows you to potentially pry into all aspects of a character's online life, as long as you can find a link to enable you to uncover each new aspect. You can look through public websites, but also snoop on messaging conversations, phone calls and email, as well as later being able to access the characters' computers themselves and have a nose around.

Certain information you come across is highlighted, what the game calls "data chunks", and you either provide these to your supervisor, or withhold them, to build a profile on someone and direct the security services to a conclusion about their guilt or innocence in the bombing.

It's a reasonable idea. However, to progress in the game, you have to throw out any common-sense notions you might have about how the information you provide will be interpreted, because it frequently defies any sense. 

The game makes it clear in the beginning that many of the "data chunks" are understood by your supervisor in their full context, but then all of a sudden something you pass along about a character referring jokingly to the "torture" of being dragged on a night out by a friend is taken completely out of context as referring to literal torture. The game tells you that information "uploads" into Orwell cannot be undone, but they also cannot be clarified.

Some "data chunks" are highlighted in a different colour, which you learn means that it conflicts with at least one other piece of information out there in cyberspace. You are only allowed to upload one of these pieces of information into the system, because it is a necessary game mechanic that the investigators cannot handle two or more possibilities for a biographic detail, so you have to pick one to send along. 

Someone might say that is how it is supposed to be, but these things feel forced as you play the game. It is especially frustrating because you often do not get any indication as to how each piece of information you decide should be taken for granted will affect what happens next.

Game events are seemingly triggered by your uploading information. This puts you in the position of uploading information you thought extraneous, or otherwise wished to withhold, in an effort to get the game to advance by finding the right trigger.

In the final act, you see written in what characters have said choices for an outcome. However, it is not clear how you are supposed to enact what I imagine for most players would be the desired outcome, nor does the character's explanation of how that outcome shall come about make sense.

Despite all of the references to Orwell's 1984, the comparison between The Nation and Oceania would be a lazy one. This is a game to suit someone who has only heard of 1984, and not actually read it. Where the extent of their understanding of the work is that that Big Brother fellow liked his surveillance. 

In the game, The Nation is authoritarian, but non-ideological. There is something about it being pro-interventionist and anti-immigration, but this does not serve as an effective allegory about real-world politics. Although the beastly Orwell programme reaches far into people's private lives, its administrators are awfully concerned with ethics and the rule of law. They have to gain legal warrants to bring someone under the scrutiny of the system, and are annoyed by your giving them extraneous personal detail. 

Although some important legal protections for the accused are absent, accused people are apparently entitled to legal representation. There is no indication that the state much cares about what people think, or that it coerces them into changing. That is, there are no thought crimes in The Nation, and state power is not arbitrary or lawless. Rather, its inhabitants appear to have have freedom of speech, thought and assembly (and, it seems from one plot point, the right to bear arms).

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell S1 is an Alternate Reality Game condensed into a single program. Big Brother deals with terrorists, and it tries to turn into a chicken and egg situation. Gameplay consists of filing clips off a mock web into a police social graph, or not. Occasionally you have to read more to resolve contradictions, which is the high point of the experience, along with a midgame sequence I shan't spoil. 

Its UI is pretty but remarkably unrefined. The keyboard shortcuts and wheel scrolling you've come to expect from browsers seem absent. The social graph will let nodes partially overlap and poorly arranges them, but you can't actually manually fix it. The base gameplay loop is spot juicy clipping on the right, open the relevant person's file on the left, then drag clipping into profile. Aliases are occasionally used, but for the vast majority of cases it's obvious who the clip is about, so the rigmarole could have been boiled down to a click. Some views overlap elements in a way the rest of the game doesn't, and dealing with that is awkward.

The finale of Season 1 came remarkably abruptly for me (about 80% too early in fact); this accidental completion meant I didn't get to deal with all as I intended.

Storywise, it works. There's a few polished plot twists and turns, and character color for several members of the cast, and the story arc goes exactly where you expect it to from the get go. It's neither subtle nor [i]Sledge Hammer![/i] in its didactisism, which is good because I expect there's few potential customers who need the lecture. The best addition was the seemingly frivolous choice of player profile picture, which got me to role play a bit an elderly, seen-it-all lady.

I estimate about 4 hours of my playtime was the main arc, and then about one more of reading the weather forecasts and such.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This one's a "buy it only on sale" for me. I would pick a neutral option were it available.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is not a game. It's more like a fancy choose your own adventure book. There is a limited number of ways that the story completes, and other than a few important decision points your actions have little consequence to how the story plays out. See the  Wikipedia page if you want to know the story before hand.  

I did not enjoy this experience, i did not find it fun, and here are my main complaints:

1) You spend all of your  time sifting through emails and texts looking for important information or data chunks. This is not a challenge because the information is highlighted for you. To make matters  even dumber, the specific emails, texts, etc are marked with an icon to show you which ones have the important information you need to act on.

2) The important decision points in the game are also highlighted in bright yellow as conflicting data chunks. You have to choose which one Orwell (the computer) will consider as fact. Often times you have to do this without any way of knowing the actual truth, but the implications of the choices are always glaringly obvious. 

3) There are data chunks that have to be given to Orwell for the story to progress, even if you don't  want to provide it. This is the one thing the ruined the experience for me, and made it obvious that the program is leading you by the nose and you have no real control. I get it. You can't read a book from the middle out, and in a "game" that is basically just a click-through-story you have to proceed in the order the author intends. All the important information has to be in place for the story to make sense. 

Lastly, and this is a minor quibble, but I also take issue with the name of this "game". Orwell is a stupidly ironic name. George Orwell was an opponent of totalitarianism, not it's champion. Perhaps a better literary subject to steal would have been Colossus (Dennis Feltham Jones). At least that Colossus was a computer.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Ultimately, my review comes down to one question:  "Would I pay for this?"  The answer is, no I don't think I would.  I can certainly see where this game would appeal to some, but it doesn't to me.  Hence, the negative score.  I don't regret playing it for free, but I don't think I would have been missing out had I not played it.

Orwell is a story game, first and foremost.  It has somewhat non-linear story to tell, where your actions will affect the details of the plot, but it'll otherwise run more or less the same, and you'll have a choice of three or four endings depending on how you do the finale.  The game tries to cover the problem of survellience but... IMO, it misses the mark completely when the tools used to spy are... indept.  More on that later.

The game boils down to reading fictional internet pages, spying on emails, calls, and texts, and snooping on people's computers.  Your goal is to find "important" information, that is pre-highlighted for you, and drag and drop what you feel is important.  The game stresses that you try to pick correct and relevant information but, ultimately, there's no failure state.  Being accurate or inaccurate only affects the plot details, nothing else, and kinda underminds the engagement of what little gameplay there is.

There's major problems with this though.  You're an investigator on a case, but your partner and the tools you're using are inept.  You can supply information, but you're often not allowed to include the context too.  Context is stupid important in real investigations, so it really undermines, well, the whole system.  You'll also come across "conflicting data", sometimes before you've even found the info it conflicts with.  A good investigator would record it all and then review it later and dismiss what's incorrect.  In Orwell?  You have to pick one.  And sometimes you have to pick blindly.  Just... why?  You also cannot collect information on individuals related to the main suspects, something I figure would be rather important.

It'll also leave you wondering one major question:  what sort of security and surveillance dystopia doesn't even have basic information, such as dates of birth and known addresses, already on file?  For a government trying to imitate 1984's Big Brother, they're failing hard at it.  Especially when around 75% of the information you're gathering is from public sources...

This here's the whole problem:  the game tries to make you question whether government observation is good or bad and whether things should be more private.  But then it puts you in the role of a guy who spends a lot of the time collecting publicly posted information and digging up stuff slower than a Google search.  Snooping into calls, computers, and bank accounts is certainly fishy, yeah, but nothing that would be legally off-limits to a police officer with a warrant in Real Life™.  And considering the plot... warrants are totally justified for everyone involved.

Orwell tries, and the story is just interesting enough for a 3-4 hour playthrough.  But... the political discussion just falls flat due to its own gameplay.  And there's games that are much better at hunting down and acquiring your information without highlighting it for you, like the parts of Hacknet focused on snooping.  

IMO:  not really worth the buy.  If you're really curious, try the demo and if you still want it, wait for a sale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Running on PopOS Linux (and this game has a linux client)... crashed on activating the first achievement.

Which is about the time I was ready to walk away from the game anyway.

Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. And a politically themed visual novel that constantly tells you and shows you what to do... that does not qualify as being a "sim". You do not need to "think" when you play Orwell, just obey orders and click where you are allowed to click... you could almost mistake it for a poetic and poignant Orwellian statement on its own existence as a "game"...  but it's not. It really is not.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I am really conflicted on this game.
On one hand, it looks and sounds excellent, being extremely stylish and immersing the player into a dystopian world of total surveillence, the characters being (mostly) well-written and felt alive. All the websites, social networks, advertisement banners and the online banter is very realistic, they even included some made-up memes for their made-up world that looked like something that could actually exist in ours. Also, had a high-quality localisation to my native language (Russian) and i didn't really feel like i was missing anything out by not playing it in its original language.

Now, on the other hand. This game mostly play out like a visual novel, where you make your choices in whether or not to upload a certain bit of marked information into the system. There are also bits with "conflicting facts" in which you also can make a choice that can affect how will the story develop. And, for the most of the game, yor choices do matter: will a certain character go to jail or manage to escape the police? Will you frame someone who made a minor break of the law into something more incriminating, so he will actually get arrested? It is incredubly nice: as a player, you feel the real power of someone with the tools for total surveillence, with only your own morals that might prevent you from abusing that power. 
The story itself plays out nicely, keeping the player in suspence, with enough of "Oh god" moments to keep you invested... right until its final part. For me, it really felt like the game did a U-turn and started pushing its morals on me, instead of letting me, as a player, to make the final choice. Sure, there are multiple endings, but all of them mostly convey the same idea (no spoilers), which, i felt, was insulting to all the choices i made before it. I expected it to be more "morally-grey", especially considering how well it started, but in the end it tried to be a lesson in how you should think. And those very same people tell us about thought crimes? Ironic.

Not recommended, unless you are fine with the game's morale.

review_text_raw:
While a good concept in reality, and not awfully executed, I find this game has two pretty blatant flaws. The narrative -  at least the little of what I experienced - seems very on the nose. As in, there is no subtly to the story they are trying to tell. Secondly, there is a fatal flaw in the game mechanic. 

The main mechanic is dragging information into a profile of someone to build up a profile of them. Fine and all, but there's two parts to the fatal flaw. Number one: You can't undo dragging in info. New info can overwrite previous info, but you cannot erase something. Secondly, context is not taken into account. During one portion I dragged in a comment from what was effectively facebook which contained a very obvious hyperbolic joke, and the profiler took it as literal and your helper agent freaked out at what the info was. This little thing absolutely killed the game for me. Without context, a way to edit it, or erase this clearly false information, the game is actively working against you when you try to profile people. The obvious counter point is 'Well the game gave you tips not to just drag in information willy nilly', but the fact it BLATANTLY ignores any context that the player sees is ridiculous.

This isn't a bad game, but between a very shallow seeming plot that basically could just be called 'The CIA watches UC Berkeley commits a Riot' and a picky core - no, let me rephrase that - ONLY mechanic, this isn't an experience I wanted to continue playing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's okay. I'm really torn on this one. There are aspects that are cool. It does make you feel like you are really part of an all-powerful government spying agency, and it did make me feel guilty for what I did at times, which is kinda the point. So in that regard I think the game achieved what it set out to. 

However, the gameplay wasn't that fun to me. The choices that you are given are pretty mundane, and some of them don't even make sense. I played it while drunk once, and I sat there for like 20 minutes trying to decide between two options, analyzing the semantics, because both were technically false depending on how you look at it. Eventually I just stopped caring and chose whatever struck me at the moment because sometimes there is no logical answer that takes all the facts into account. Your choices do have an impact for sure, but because of the wording of some of the options, it isn't really clear what you are choosing. Given that it is basically a visual novel, I wouldn't expect the gameplay to be amazing. But I would at least hope for some robust choices, and a riveting storyline. Well, while the premise is interesting, the actual storyline involves mostly frivolous details about the characters and their lives without really making me bond enough with any of them to actually care all that much, so it ended up being kinda boring after the novelty wore off, honestly.

Also, I have to say I didn't really find the world they built very believable. They basically portrayed a totalitarian police state world within the framework of our existing politics to some degree, and it doesn't really make sense. For example, the terrorists all seem to be left wing communist types. Fair enough. But they are kinda portrayed in a positive light, like they are fighting for freedom. But really, they don't want freedom, it seems they idolize communist dictators, so they just want THEIR side to be the totalitarian state. Which makes sense in a way, but then why all the rhetoric about freedom? If you want communism, you really don't care about freedom. And they portray the totalitarian government as conservative. Interesting choice, given that modern conservatives are the ones speaking up for free speech and lower taxes and stuff. Oh yeah, and the totalitarian government wants to lower taxes. Umm, okay? If you have a totalitarian government that can rule with an iron fist, why bother lowering taxes? Don't you need lots of money so you can have all these government programs to run people's lives? As a bit of a politics junkie, the way they built the political landscape has a lot of ideological inconsistencies, is basically what I am saying. I'm not saying it's impossible that there would be a conservative totalitarian regime. But that would come with a specific set of beliefs. They wouldn't be pushing for family values for example. Ever read "Brave New World"? Defeating the family and community structures is key to politically subjugating the population. I could go on, but basically, because of the inconsistencies, I found myself being pulled out of the experience.

Also, there is some weird plot point that tries to tie in this semi-fictional, semi-real world into the actual real world? That part is pretty confusing and I think they could have left it out because it doesn't add anything IMO and it just makes less sense the more you think about it. I think they should have gone all in on a completely fictional world, with a completely different society instead of trying to tie it in in weird ways like making the terrorists left wing punk rock vegan types, and the totalitarian government conservative family types, with all the baggage that comes along with those stereotypes. Think about 1984 and Brave New World. I'm pretty sure that the authors went out of their ways to make sure that no political archetypes were projected onto the characters because that would take people out of the story and into debates about modern-day politics. They would have done well to do the same here. Just make a broader point without muddying the waters with tribalism.

Honestly, I would probably give it a 5.5/10. It's interesting for a little while, so I guess it's good that it's not very long. I had no desire to play it over and see different endings, frankly I was a bit relieved when it was over. So, maybe I should be giving it a hesitant thumbs up... But because I'm so torn on it, and the other reviews are so positive, I'm gonna have to give it a thumbs down to get it closer to where I think it should be.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
As much as I admire technical aspects and writing in the game, I strongly recommend you to avoid buying it. The game tells a modern story about a survelliance state. This is a divisive and complicated topic. It would have been nice if the game went though the pros and cons of survelliance and then let the player decide on their own.

Instead, the game's message is one-sided and biased: "Survelliance is bad, BAD, BAAD; it's a corrupt tool built by corrupt people, therefore BURN IT". I'm very sad to see such treatment. It is a very dangerous message. I'm not saying survelliance is a shining white knight of good, but it's not a dark super-villain either. Like any thing in life it's shades of grey, and everyone has to decide on their own. The game does not let you to. It pretends to, but gives you a choice between a few shades of black instead.
